newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin's health of dwindling import for dollar.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's health of dwindling import for dollar.

text.p: Rumors that Russian leader Boris Yeltsin's poor health had worsened -- once a primary source of fodder for currency markets -- caused barely a ripple in the dollar on Wednesday.

After many months of secrecy shrouding Yeltsin's health, currency traders had deeply discounted Yeltsin's heart troubles even before the Kremlin opted for a policy of fuller disclosure earlier this year.
"There are a couple of bigger issues on the table now," said David Durrant, senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A.
"The market has dealt with it long enough. It is not going to have the effect it would have had even in August."

Yeltin's press office quickly denied financial market rumors that he had died, saying the president was working at the Barvikha sanatorium, outside Moscow, where he has been resting since last weekend in preparation for heart surgery.

The Swiss franc strengthened briefly, but the dollar wavered between 1.5270 and 1.5310 marks after the rumors, which swirled through the U.S. and London markets on Wednesday. It failed to even challenge the boundaries of its recent narrow trading bands.

Although the constitutional mechanism of transferring power is considered murky, Yeltsin has already yielded much day to day control and some traders said the liberalization of Russia's capital markets would probably not be jeopardized by his death.

"It's not relevant," said James Fitzgibbons, currency strategist at ING Capital Markets. "Is that going to change the process that's continually occurring in Russia? No. Are they going to default on their deutschemark denominated liabilities because of of him? No."

The bigger risk is that, under Yeltsin's successors, democracy in Russia fails to firmly take root over time and that increasing national debt derails the train before the country becomes truly capitalist, traders said.
While Yeltsin works a few hours a day, he has ceded many of his daily tasks to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

The President met his prime minister at the sanatorium on Tuesday. His press office issued a statement on border policies on Wednesday in which Yeltsin said Russia had no territorial claims on other countries.
In the event of Yeltsin's death, Russia's constitution states the prime minister would become acting-president for three months, but then a general election for the presidency must be held.
But some analysts do worry that a general election could result in a less market-friendly politician taking the helm.

"I could imagine a group taking control of Russia who want to go back to earlier borders, or get a little hostile to NATO expansion towards the east," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "I could see someone taking over who could renege on some of their debt."
Chandler said that, if Yeltsin died suddenly, the markets would probably sell the mark and buy dollars and Swiss francs in a knee-jerk reaction.
But the longer-term reaction to the hypothetical event would depend on the political fallout, traders said.

"If you tell me no power struggle and his prime minister and other liberal-type refomers take over, then little change," said Chandler. "But, if you tell me (security chief Alexander) Lebed is going to take over, I would say a different market reaction.
"A lot would depend on how the dust settles."
In either case, experts said the market may be too distracted by events in Europe and Japan to bet indiscriminately on the mysterious present or future exercise of power in the Kremlin.
"It appears there are bigger things on the table today than Yeltsin," said I.D.E.A's Durrant. "You know, convergence hiccups...in Europe and elections going on in Japan."
